# Codex Security Cloud includes Daybreak Blue at DevDay; what still needs approval and review


By OpenTools Team


OpenAI's DevDay update presents Codex Security Cloud on desktop and web with Daybreak Blue models available inside Cloud, without a separate application. The scanner and its plan categories predate DevDay; repository setup, paid‑scan opt‑in and human review still matter.


##


Daybreak access inside Cloud is the useful change


OpenAI's[September 29 DevDay recap](https://openai.com/index/devday-2026-recap/) presents Codex Security Cloud for Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu users on desktop and web. It says the Cloud product includes access to models offered through Daybreak Blue without a separate Daybreak application. That removes one product‑specific application step for eligible defenders, but does not mean every use of a Daybreak model is automatically approved. The[current Codex Security help page](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001107-codex-security) says the included access applies within Cloud; it does not grant Daybreak Blue access in other Codex Security products or through the API.


Codex Security itself and these plan categories are older. OpenAI[introduced the research preview on March 6](https://openai.com/index/codex-security-now-in-research-preview/) to Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu customers through Codex web, and its[August Daybreak workflow guide](https://developers.openai.com/blog/scaling-cyber-defenders-with-daybreak) already described connected GitHub repositories, continuing Cloud scans and proposed patches. DevDay describes desktop as well as web access and clarifies the included cyber‑model path inside Cloud. Treating the scanner or plan eligibility as a September invention would obscure what actually changed for a security team.[TechCrunch's launch‑day reporting](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/29/openai-gives-codex-reusable-cloud-environments-that-work-across-devices/) also describes Daybreak access without a separate application; it does not independently establish that scans find or fix vulnerabilities better.


##


What happens after you connect a repository


The[DevDay recap](https://openai.com/index/devday-2026-recap/) describes whole‑GitHub‑repository scans on demand or on a schedule, plus ongoing checks when new commits arrive. Codex then investigates candidate findings, removes duplicates and prepares fixes in the cloud while the developer's laptop is closed. The[help article](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001107-codex-security) makes the workflow more concrete: Cloud connects to selected GitHub repositories, builds an editable threat model around entry points, trust boundaries and sensitive paths, and can scan the repository or its commits. It attempts to validate potential vulnerabilities in an isolated environment before surfacing findings.


The important boundary is between a proposed fix and a changed codebase. OpenAI says Codex Security does not automatically modify the repository: it proposes a patch for human review, which can be turned into a pull request. Its[August developer guide](https://developers.openai.com/blog/scaling-cyber-defenders-with-daybreak) recommends inspecting code evidence, attack paths, reproduction output and remediation guidance, then reviewing a proposed diff before applying it. A team can use a small, lower‑risk repository and a dedicated reviewer group to judge the finding quality before enabling continuing scans across critical services. Neither OpenAI's product descriptions nor this article is a hands‑on test of a particular repository's vulnerability coverage.


##


Plan eligibility, Cloud funding and Daybreak rights are separate decisions


A Pro or qualifying workspace plan is only the first gate. The[current setup guidance](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001107-codex-security) requires connecting and enabling the GitHub repositories a team wants to scan; Enterprise and Edu admins also control Codex Cloud and Codex Security permissions through workspace roles. It describes Codex Security as a research preview, so the access list should not be read as a general‑availability guarantee or proof that every account has completed setup.


There is also a cost boundary. The[help article](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001107-codex-security) says Security Cloud uses token‑based billing, existing customers must receive notice and opt in before paid usage begins, and scans pause if funding is unavailable. The Daybreak Blue inclusion does not erase those scan costs or confer API access. Before enabling a recurring scan, a lead should check the workspace's permissions and funding, define the repositories and commit scope, and assign a person to review the generated threat model and findings. For broader platform context, OpenTools has a[Codex tool record](https://opentools.ai/tools/codex) connected to its[OpenAI organization](https://opentools.ai/organizations/openai) ; this DevDay change is a dated security workflow update, not a newly identified foundation model or a benchmark result.
